title: Denmark ratifies Trump security deal over Greenland after months of diplomatic tensions
description: Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen (sitting, R) attends the second legislative process and vote on the security agreement between Denmark
body: Denmark's Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen (sitting, R) attends the second legislative process and vote on the security agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the US in the Parliament Hall at Christiansborg in Copenhagen, on November 19, 2026.Mads Claus Rasmussen | Afp | Getty ImagesDanish lawmakers on Thursday approved a security agreement with U.S. President Donald Trump covering Greenland, seeking to end months of strained diplomatic tensions over the island's future.Trump and the prime ministers of Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September. It allows Washington to expand its military presence on the island, paving the way for two new bases and the construction of a "Golden Dome" missile defense system.Thursday's approval follows a protracted period in which Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the self-governing Danish territory. Tensions reached fever pitch in January as the president repeatedly insisted that the U.S. needed Greenland for its national security, at times declining to rule out using military force to acquire it.A parliamentary tally showed 109 Danish lawmakers unanimously backed the agreement on Thursday, per Reuters. Greenland's parliament ratified the deal earlier this month. It is not subject to a vote in the U.S. Senate.NEW YORK, NEW YORK - SEPTEMBER 22: (L-R) U.S. President Donald Trump, Prime Minister of Denmark Mette Frederiksen and Prime Minister of Greenland Jens-Frederik Nielsen hold up the proclamations during the signing of a security pact between the U.S., Denmark, and Greenland during the 81st session of the United Nations (U.N.) General Assembly at U.N. Headquarters on September 22, 2026 in New York City.  Chip Somodevilla | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesThe Danish government can now formally notify the U.S. that both parliaments have consented to complete the ratification process.The deal supplements an existing 1951 defense agreement. It also maintains Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.Trump's proposed Golden Dome is a multibillion-dollar initiative designed to shield the U.S. from a range of aerial and missile threats. It was rolled out in May last year and is often compared with Israel's "Iron Dome" system.Trump's threats alarmed Greenlanders and other Europeans and opened a rift between the U.S. and NATO, of which Denmark and the U.S. are both members. Greenland has maintained that it is not for sale, and the European Union earlier this year united to rebuke Trump. — CNBC's Kevin Breuninger & Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Denmark ratifies Trump security deal over Greenland after months of diplomatic tensions

title: 3-step method to influence people and win them over, from a Stanford expert: ‘Your voice is like a muscle’
description: Think back on the most memorable, inspiring speeches or presentations you've witnessed. They probably weren't delivered in a monotone, Matt Abrahams s
body: Think back on the most memorable, inspiring speeches or presentations you've witnessed. They probably weren't delivered in a monotone, Matt Abrahams says."The human brain is designed to pick out and focus on things that are novel and new," says Abrahams, a Stanford University lecturer on strategic communication and host of the "Think Fast, Talk Smart" podcast. "So anything that stays the same, like a monotonous voice or cadence, we don't pay as much attention to."Indeed, successful leaders often have an uncanny ability to win over a crowd: The power of persuasion lies not just in what you actually have to say, but also in how you say it, research shows. The topic has taken on new relevance this week as Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress steps into one of the most closely watched leadership roles in corporate America.In appearances this week, including Nvidia's quarterly earnings call and an interview with CNBC's "Mad Money" host Jim Cramer, Kress has discussed the company's performance. She's also addressed employees and investors in a time of leadership upheaval, following Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang's high-profile resignation on Nov. 12.How Kress communicates has drawn attention and, in some circles, criticism. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal described her public speaking style as "slow, steady, almost monotone." That doesn't necessarily make it ineffective. Her situation, however, highlights a broader challenge leaders face when they need to inform, reassure and persuade large groups of people at once.Generally speaking, anyone can stand a better chance at persuading others to follow them by honing an engaging speaking style, says Abrahams. Some people may be naturally expressive and engaging. For others, it's a skill that requires time and practice.Abrahams suggests a three-step playbook for anyone learning to speak more persuasively: "repetition, reflection and feedback."3 steps to influence people with your voice: 'Repetition, reflection and feedback'Abrahams' simplest advice for making yourself a more engaging speaker: "When you're using emotive words, reflect the emotion in them." That means adding some emphasis to words like "exciting," "huge" or "challenging," and so on. If you tend to speak monotonously, leaning into obviously emotive words can help you vary your tone and inflection enough to keep your audience's attention.There's a catch, of course: People find inauthenticity off-putting and disingenuous, says Abrahams. Don't alter your voice entirely, he suggests — just add some variety to your intonation and speaking volume. Learning to do so while still sounding natural takes practice, he notes."Your voice is like a muscle," says Abrahams. "You can train it. You can grow it [and] strengthen it, just like you go to the gym to lift weights."Practicing repetition starts with reading aloud from a chosen text, which Abrahams recommends so you don't have to overthink what you're saying. And the same way you might lift heavy weights to get stronger, Abrahams suggests reading overly expressive material to start getting out of your comfort zone and practice being energetic and engaging. He instructs his Stanford students to try reading Dr. Seuss books, as their playful words and bouncy rhymes can naturally make for a lively performance. While practicing reading out loud, record yourself to watch and listen to later, Abrahams recommends. Then, use the recording to reflect on what works and what doesn't, and incorporate your self-feedback into your next reading. You can also play the recording for a few trusted peers to get their thoughts, Abrahams says.If a line reading doesn't sound natural in your voice, feels flat or even rushed, keep trying it until you're satisfied, he says. Leaders are often asked to deliver lengthy speeches or talk for long periods in interviews and panels, so it's important to build your vocal stamina, he adds."We have to calibrate ourselves," he says.Abrahams asks his Stanford graduate students to review their recordings in three ways, he says:With no sound, so they can focus on their physical presenceWith sound only, so they can dissect their vocal deliveryAll together, to review the full performance"That's how you train your brain to see: 'What do I need to sound like?'" says Abrahams.

schema.headline: 3-step method to influence people and win them over, from a Stanford expert: ‘Your voice is like a muscle’

title: Congress passes bill to protect older investors from financial fraud
description: Ekaterina Demidova | Moment | Getty ImagesBipartisan legislation aimed at protecting older Americans and other vulnerable adults from financial fraud
body: Ekaterina Demidova | Moment | Getty ImagesBipartisan legislation aimed at protecting older Americans and other vulnerable adults from financial fraud has cleared Congress, putting it on track to become law.Called the Financial Exploitation Prevention Act of 2025 and passed by the House in June, H.R. 2478 was approved by unanimous consent in the Senate Wednesday night — meaning no senators objected to its passage.The measure will next head to President Donald Trump's desk. The White House did not respond to a CNBC request for comment on whether Trump plans to sign the bill into law.Read more CNBC personal finance coverageHow to get Anthropic stock — without buying the IPOThere's a growing 'property tax revolt' as homeowners face rising costsSocial Security could pay benefits until 2059 if payroll kept pace with GDP: AARPCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026The bill would generally allow mutual fund companies and their transfer agents, which handle shareholder records and transactions, to temporarily delay paying out redemption requests when they suspect an older or otherwise vulnerable investor is being financially exploited."Financial exploitation can have devastating consequences for victims and their families," said Erin Koeppel, a managing director and government relations and public policy counsel at the CFP Board, the organization that oversees the certified financial planner certification. "This legislation fills an important regulatory gap that can help protect vulnerable investors before assets are lost."Reported fraud among older adults hit $3 billion in 2025The measure's congressional approval comes amid growing financial fraud among older Americans. Those age 60 or older reported losing about $3 billion to fraud in 2025, a 25% increase from $2.4 billion in 2024, according to the Federal Trade Commission's latest report to Congress on fraud among older adults, which was released in October. That amount is 400% higher than the $600 million reported lost in 2020."Generally, we support all legislation that aims to prevent any form of financial elder abuse," said Bob Blancato, national coordinator for the Elder Justice Coalition, an advocacy group.While just 6% of older fraud victims reported losing $100,000 or more in 2025, those losses accounted for 70% of the age group's total reported losses. The number of people reporting losses of that magnitude rose nearly sixfold to 6,769 in 2025, from 1,136 in 2020.However, because many scams go unreported, the FTC estimates actual losses in 2025 could have been anywhere from $13.3 billion to $119.5 billion. In 2024, the estimated range was from $10.1 billion to $81.5 billion.watch nowScammers are increasingly targeting Americans' life savings by impersonating banks, businesses and government agencies, according to the FTC. The schemes often involve fabricated emergencies that convince victims to transfer money to supposedly protect their accounts from being compromised.Additionally, content created by artificial intelligence that can help criminals carry out schemes is becoming increasingly difficult to detect and easier to make, according to the FBI.What the Financial Exploitation Prevention Act doesUnder the Financial Exploitation Prevention Act, mutual fund companies and their transfer agents could temporarily postpone payments when they reasonably believe a redemption request involves financial exploitation.This would apply to investors age 65 and older, as well as younger adults reasonably believed to have a mental or physical impairment that prevents them from protecting their own interests.Companies could initially delay paying out redemption proceeds for up to 15 business days. They could extend the hold by another 10 business days if they still reasonably believe exploitation already occurred, is underway or was attempted. State regulators, certain government agencies or courts could also extend the hold.How a 'trusted contact' may help thwart fraudThe bill also addresses the use of a "trusted contact" — an individual whom financial firms can contact when concerns arise about an investor's account. That person may be able to intervene to prevent the fraud by reaching out to the account holder.Mutual fund companies that opt into the new protections would be required to ask customers to provide the name and contact information of at least one trusted contact.The legislation would build on existing investor protections. Already, the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, or FINRA, permits brokerage firms to temporarily place holds on certain transactions if they suspect financial exploitation of an older or otherwise vulnerable investor.Additionally, FINRA requires brokerages to make a reasonable effort to add a trusted contact to accounts, although investors are not required to provide one. Many banks and other financial institutions also ask account holders for a trusted contact.Taxes paid on some fraud targeted in separate billSeparately, another House-passed bipartisan bill that aims to provide some relief for certain scam victims is awaiting action in the Senate. That measure, the Tax Relief for Fraud Victims Act, is intended to prevent people who lose money to scams from suffering additional financial harm through the federal tax system.The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 temporarily limited deductions for personal theft losses, and Trump's "big beautiful bill" of 2025 made those limits permanent. Some investment scam losses may still be deductible, but losses from some romance and impersonation scams generally aren't, according to a 2025 IRS memo. Victims who withdraw money from a traditional 401(k) or IRA may also owe income tax on the withdrawal and, if they're under 59½, possibly a 10% early-withdrawal penalty.The Tax Relief for Fraud Victims Act, H.R. 9500, would repeal those deduction limits and waive the 10% penalty on withdrawals tied to deductible fraud losses. The House passed it 408-17 in September, and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee. It's unclear whether the Senate will take it up before this Congress ends."We would hope ... the Senate will join the House in passing H.R. 9500 to end another form of elder financial abuse," Blancato said.

schema.headline: Congress passes bill to protect older investors from financial fraud

title: California attorney general issues Nvidia subpoena in probe of China chip diversion
description: Rob Bonta, attorney general of California, speaks during a news conference in Oakland, California, US, on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026.David Paul Morris | B
body: Rob Bonta, attorney general of California, speaks during a news conference in Oakland, California, US, on Tuesday, Aug. 18, 2026.David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesCalifornia Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia on Thursday as part of a probe of whether the company's advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China in contravention of U.S. export restrictions, his office said.The probe comes a week after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy. Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that is being investigation for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China."The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a statement."My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law," Bonta said."Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," the attorney general said.Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bonta's subpoena.Nvidia shares are down 22% in the nine trading days since Huang admitted to an extramarital affair. The stock is on pace for its seventh straight weekly loss, shedding 38% of its value over that stretch.

schema.headline: California attorney general issues Nvidia subpoena in probe of China chip diversion

title: Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?
description: Anthropic signage during the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, Nov. 19, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty I
body: Anthropic signage during the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York, Nov. 19, 2026.Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesAnthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.It wasn't supposed to play out this way. Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech. But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year."You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes."The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3." While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market."There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets. Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade. "If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks. Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

schema.headline: Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

title: APEC final day in photos: Trump, Xi and Putin shake hands; Takaichi kept at a distance
description: US President Donald Trump (L) is greeted by China's President Xi Jinping before a bilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacifi
body: US President Donald Trump (L) is greeted by China's President Xi Jinping before a bilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong province, on November 19, 2026.  Carlos Barria | Afp | Getty ImagesWorld leaders including the U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin gathered Thursday for the second day of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, ahead of a historic trilateral meeting between the U.S., Russia and China later in the day.International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva kicked off Thursday's agenda after China's President Xi Jinping's welcome note. Georgieva said that artificial intelligence and energy supply shocks had accelerated global inflation in many economies, calling for monetary policy tightening.  Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi was met with another cold reception. She spent several minutes trying to talk to Xi who did not appear to respond with no interpreter present. Trump held separate bilateral meetings with Putin and Xi earlier in the day. The president praised Xi's leadership and said Washington was negotiating deals with several major APEC economies.  In their first in-person talks in over a year, Trump told Putin that "We've known each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or at least start," referring to Putin as a "friend." The three leaders are due to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting later Thursday, with the Middle East conflict, Russia's war in Ukraine, trade and artificial intelligence likely on the agenda. Expectations for the historic three-way meeting to yield any concrete outcome remain low.The summit will conclude Trump's whirlwind Asia trip, after which the American president will return to Washington, D.C.Here are the highlights in photos from the second and final day of the APEC summit: U.S. President Donald Trump, front row center, speaks with Xi Jinping, China's president, front row title: Japan core inflation soars to highest this year as energy subsidy expiry pushes up consumer prices
description: People shop in a supermarket in Tokyo on May 23, 2025.    Philip Fong | Afp | Getty ImagesCore inflation in Japan soared to a fresh high in 2026, comi
body: People shop in a supermarket in Tokyo on May 23, 2025.    Philip Fong | Afp | Getty ImagesCore inflation in Japan soared to a fresh high in 2026, coming in at 2.2% in October as higher energy costs and their knock-on effects pushed up prices in the wider economy. Core inflation, which strips out prices of food, was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists, but was higher than the 2.1% in prior month.Headline inflation came in at 2.3% compared with September's 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which strips out prices of fresh food and energy, dipped slightly to 2.2% from 2.4% in the month before, government data released on Friday showed. Energy subsidies for households expired in September, exposing consumers to higher prices brought about by the Iran war. Energy prices climbed 2.2% in October, a sharp spike from the 0.6% decline in September. Gas prices jumped 5.8% compared to the 2.4% rise the month before. Fuel, light and water charges also saw a considerable acceleration, increasing 3.4% compared to last month's 0.8%. Following the release, the Nikkei 225 index was down 2.1%, while the 10-year JGB yield fell 2 basis points to 2.805%.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconJapan has reportedly approved reintroduction of energy subsidies in December to stave off higher imported energy prices as higher prices crimp growth, hitting consumption and net exports.The October inflation reading is likely to push the Bank of Japan toward another rate hike in December, despite an unexpected contraction in economic growth in the third quarter. Data from LSEG indicates that there is a 72% chance of a 25 basis point hike from the Bank of Japan.On Wednesday, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament that the central bank was also "mindful" of the weak yen and rising crude prices, saying that these could hurt ⁠households' real income and weigh on consumption more than expected. The yen marginally strengthened to trade at 159.59 against the dollar after the data release.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconJapan's inflation is likely to still stay above 2% for the rest of 2026 and into the first quarter of 2027, according to Ma Tieying, senior economist at DBS Group Research. She pointed out that while higher energy prices and yen weakness have contributed to headline inflation, the recent upturn is also supported by domestic factors."Wage growth has remained above 3% for nine consecutive months, pointing to a broader pickup in underlying inflation as stronger wage gains feed through to services prices and household spending. This suggests a more durable wage–price cycle is taking hold."Ma expects the BOJ to raise rates in its December meeting, then twice more in 2027, bringing its terminal rate to 2%.

schema.headline: Japan core inflation soars to highest this year as energy subsidy expiry pushes up consumer prices

title: AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure
description: watch nowShares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report al
body: watch nowShares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."CNBC did not independently verify this information.Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."Stock Chart IconStock chart iconAMD, 1-dayThe allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia. "The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

schema.headline: AMD dives on short seller report of alleged China exposure

title: One of the world's most contested seas is proving too much for Asia's leaders to resolve
description: Activists display anti-China placards and flags during a protest at a park in Manila on June 18, 2019, after a Chinese vessel last week collided with
body: Activists display anti-China placards and flags during a protest at a park in Manila on June 18, 2019, after a Chinese vessel last week collided with a Philippine fishing boat which sank in the disputed South China Sea and sailed away sparking outrage. Photo by TED ALJIBE / AFP) (Photo by TED ALJIBE/AFP via Getty Images)Ted Aljibe | Afp | Getty ImagesOne of the world's most contested bodies of water continues to cause problems for Asia's leaders.A substantive Code of Conduct in the South China Sea does not seem to be feasible despite ASEAN nations expressing optimism that the negotiations could finally conclude after more than two decades, experts told CNBC. The ASEAN summit in the Philippines failed to resolve it, despite Manila saying it intended to conclude the Code this year. The crux of the issue is that China claims virtually all of the South China Sea as its own territory, despite international rulings saying it's not the case and historical claims from many other countries. China's "nine-dash line" claim was ruled as invalid by the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 2016, although Beijing has refused to recognize that ruling.This illustration taken on March 19, 2025 shows the nine-dash line on a map of a disputed area of the South China Sea on a laptop in Lao Cai province.    Nhac Nguyen | Afp | Getty ImagesOver decades, China has been building shoals into structures that strengthen its territorial assertions, and has become increasingly aggressive in policing the territory against nations such as the Philippines, that claim traditional rights over the maritime areas.The Code of Conduct for the South China Sea aims to address areas where multiple ASEAN nations and China have disputes and competing claims. Manila has reported that it had completed 80% of the negotiating text, with negotiations to continue under next ASEAN chair Singapore. But, experts are skeptical that a "substantive and effective" agreement can be realized, at least in the short term. "It's an annual ritual. The ASEAN Chair commits to completing the Code of Conduct in January, but by November is reporting that — although great progress has been made — they didn't quite get there this year. Rinse, repeat," Ray Powell, executive director at gray-zone activities tracker SeaLight Foundation told CNBC.He described the 80% number as "a meaningless statistic," given that the issue at hand was complex and contentious. ASEAN secretary general Kao Kim Hourn still sees potential for resolution. "I don't think it's a failure at all," he told CNBC's JP Ong. "There's still a lot of commitment and a lot of leadership on both sides to move ahead and get it done."watch nowBut Collin Koh, senior fellow at the Institute of Defence and Strategic Studies in Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told CNBC that even if 80% of the text has been set, the 20% remaining contain the most persistent problems, including geographical scope, competing interests among ASEAN member states, and enforcement.Koh said the original aim was ASEAN to negotiate with China "one-to-one," but, it has never been the case. "It has always been 10 against one. Now you add Timor Leste. Now 11 against one. So, because of that, there is never any unified ASEAN position that they will bring to the table with with China," he pointed out.Disputes in the South China Sea stretch at least as far back as the 1970s, with various countries such as Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam claiming various zones and islands in the critical maritime region, which houses rich natural resources and fishing areas. 'Unlikely to happen'Back in 2015, Singapore has positioned itself as a "neutral broker" in ASEAN-China dialogue, with then-Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong saying that Singapore will deal "fairly and openly with all parties" in order to "preserve peace and stability in the region." "China at its heart doesn't really want a code of conduct, and it continues to push more assertively into the South China Sea."Joshua KurlantzickSenior Fellow, Southeast Asia and South Asia, Council on Foreign RelationsBut while the city-state may be able to broker some compromises, the disagreements that have held up the code for almost a quarter of a century will persist, according to Lynn Kuok, Lee Kuan Yew Chair of Southeast Asia Studies at the Brookings Institution. "Beijing, moreover, has little incentive to accept meaningful restraints while it continues to consolidate its position in the South China Sea," Kuok added.  Her view was echoed by Joshua Kurlantzick, senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, who said that a code of conduct is unlikely to happen soon, if ever. "China at its heart doesn't really want a code of conduct, and it continues to push more assertively into the South China Sea." He pointed out Beijing's actions against the Philippines in the region, including around the disputed Scarborough Shoal. Chinese coast guard vessels have most recently been accused of ramming Filipino fishing vessels near the Spratly islands in September, and have used lasers and water cannons against Filipino ships in the past. Kurlantzick also said that there are multiple countries within ASEAN that are close to China that are willing to hold up any agreement on the Code, adding that the move toward China is also happening as the U.S.' commitment to defense in the region becomes less clear."I do not think there is really any chance of a code of conduct happening with Singapore as ASEAN chair — or really, anyone as ASEAN chair," he said.At the same time, a rushed or flawed Code would be worse than none at all, Powell said."In fact, the worst outcome is not a failure to agree, but rather a weak Code that would enable Beijing to undermine UNCLOS," he said. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which came into force in 1994, provides a comprehensive legal framework for oceans and seas globally."The narrative from China could then be 'see, now we have this shiny new regional agreement that overrides that problematic law invented by outsiders who don't understand East Asia and shouldn't have a say here anyway,'" Powell added.—CNBC's Joanna Ossinger contributed to this article.

schema.headline: One of the world's most contested seas is proving too much for Asia's leaders to resolve

title: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion
description: The logo of the Italian technology company Bending Spoons SpA is pictured on the facade of the company's headquarters on November 16, 2026 in Milan, I
body: The logo of the Italian technology company Bending Spoons SpA is pictured on the facade of the company's headquarters on November 16, 2026 in Milan, Italy.Emanuele Cremaschi | Getty ImagesTax software maker Intuit said Thursday that it has agreed to sell marketing subsidiary Mailchimp to Italian technology consolidator Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion in cash and stock. The deal is set to close in early 2027, according to a statement.The sale is a costly retreat for Intuit, which paid $12 billion for Mailchimp in 2021 in a push beyond its core tax and accounting businesses. Five years later, the software maker is unloading the email-marketing company for less than one-third of that price after Mailchimp became a drag on its overall revenue growth.The deal is the latest instance of Bending Spoons picking up a once promising technology asset. The company bought productivity software startup Airtable in September for 10% of what it was once worth.The Bending Spoons portfolio also contains AOL, Brightcove, Eventbrite, Evernote, Meetup, Vimeo, and WeTransfer. In August Intuit started running Mailchimp as a distinct operating segment. The move was meant to give investors more transparency as the company tried to manage the unit for profitability, Sandeep Aujla, Intuit's finance chief, said at a September company briefing.Also on Thursday, Intuit announced stronger-than-expected earnings and revenue for its fiscal first quarter, which ended on Oct. 31. The company reported $2.91 in adjusted earnings per share on $4.35 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG were looking for $2.70 per share and $4.31 billion in revenue. While Intuit's revenue increased 12% year over year, Mailchimp revenue declined 1% to $313 million. Analysts polled by StreetAccount had expected $314.4 million.Management called for $22.88 to $23.12 in adjusted earnings per share for the 2027 fiscal year, with $23.081 billion to $23.365 billion in revenue. Analysts polled by LSEG had predicted $23.62 in adjusted earnings per share on $23.43 billion in revenue. Intuit shares tumbled 15% in extended trading.The company said Mailchimp should produce $1.256 billion to $1.266 billion in fiscal 2027 revenue, which would be down 1% to flat year over year. In August Aujla said Intuit anticipated Mailchimp's higher effective prices offsetting increased client churn. Mailchimp was founded in 2001. Rivals include Klaviyo, which went public in 2023.Berkshire Hathaway invested $600 million in Bending Spoons when the acquirer went public in July, and in October Bending Spoons said Berkshire invested another $330 million.WATCH: Intuit shares fall on guidancewatch now

schema.headline: Intuit to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for $3.68 billion

title: Amazon app warns New York of higher costs if Mamdani delivery law passes
description: An Amazon driver loads packages into a delivery van at an Amazon delivery station in Alpharetta, Georgia, Nov. 28, 2022.Justin Sullivan | Getty Images
body: An Amazon driver loads packages into a delivery van at an Amazon delivery station in Alpharetta, Georgia, Nov. 28, 2022.Justin Sullivan | Getty ImagesAmazon is taking its fight against a New York City delivery bill, which has been backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, to its shopping website and app. Some users who open the company's shopping app or website report being served with pop-ups and banners warning that the New York City Council "could add up to $5 per order" if it passes Intro 518, or the Delivery Protection Act. The bill would require Amazon to employ its army of third-party delivery companies directly, disrupting the contractor model it has relied on since 2018. Amazon uses a network of thousands of small companies, which often work solely for Amazon, to handle the last-mile portion of shipments, in an effort to speed up deliveries and control more of its logistics operations. "If this legislation passes, we'd no longer be able to work with them, and we'd be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city," Amazon's in-app message states. "That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees."The proposed legislation was introduced in February and is awaiting review by City Council Speaker Julie Menin.Amazon also posted a statement on its company website where it often publishes its policy positions. But rarely has the company used its valuable e-commerce site and app real estate to push its perspectives. Other tech companies including Uber and Lyft have similarly used their apps to advocate for or against legislation in the past. Amazon's pop-up notices and a stationary banner on its store homepage direct users to a form where they can "contact your council member to oppose Intro 518." According to Amazon, 20,000 customers sent emails to city council members in the first six hours that the pop-up appeared.Menin told CNBC in a statement that Amazon's claim it will need to raise prices due to the proposed legislation "defies logic." "We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs," Menin said. "If Amazon thinks this deceptive campaign will effectively threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council, they are dead wrong." Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said in a statement that the company put up the notices to be "transparent with our customers" about what the bill "would cause them if it passes as written." "If customers are concerned, one of the most impactful things they can do is contact their City Council member and ask them to oppose this bill," Nantel said. The Delivery Protection Act has received a swell of support from labor groups, including the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which has sought to unionize Amazon delivery and warehouse workers. Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon's subcontractor model "leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets." He's argued the bill would lead to safer working conditions for drivers, and allow the city to "regulate last-mile operations." Amazon disputed Mamdani's claims, saying the bill would put Delivery Service Partner jobs "at risk without improving safety." It also argued that other businesses and governments use contractors in their operations, and said the DSP model has allowed it to meet growing customer demand."It works because local entrepreneurs — people rooted in their communities — deliver a better experience," Amazon said. "They invest in their teams, their routes, and their neighborhoods. That's not a liability play." Amazon has lobbied heavily against the bill, while logistics and business groups have launched local advertising campaigns, and warned they may sue the city if the bill passes.

schema.headline: Amazon app warns New York of higher costs if Mamdani delivery law passes

title: Trump, Xi, Putin said they plan to boost oil production, revamp UN after trilateral talks
description: watch nowThe U.S., China and Russia on Thursday vowed to boost production of petroleum products and reaffirmed their commitment to reducing nuclear ri
body: watch nowThe U.S., China and Russia on Thursday vowed to boost production of petroleum products and reaffirmed their commitment to reducing nuclear risks following their leaders' historic trilateral summit.President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin "had an in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation and committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the countries said in identical statements shared after the meeting in Shenzhen, China.The statements were brief and broad, containing few details about what the leaders agreed on during their talks. They did not include any mention of Russia's war against Ukraine, which continues to rage in eastern Europe despite recent U.S. efforts to broker a ceasefire. They also made no reference to the U.S.' war in Iran, in which Russia and China have both been accused of aiding Tehran."The three countries plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations. They reaffirmed the importance of stable energy flows," according to the statements, described as a "Heads of State Declaration toward Peace."The three presidents also "reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought," and committed to a "dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons."And they committed to "reform" the United Nations so it "can respond more effectively to global challenges and conform to its fundamental mission of international peace and security," according to the statements.The leaders also agreed that "the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction," the declarations stated. The Trump administration has heavily criticized the ICC, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month announced new U.S. sanctions against what he called a "rogue court."In opening remarks earlier Thursday, Trump said the U.S., Russia and China are "uniquely positioned" to reduce the world's nuclear weapons stockpile."As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on earth and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said."The power is unbelievable, unthinkable," he said, adding that it's "a very hard thing" for countries to reduce nuclear weapons.That would include not letting Iran have nuclear weapons, Trump said. He said the three leaders would also discuss the war between Russia and Ukraine, and criticized "rogue globalist organizations," including the International Criminal Court. The closely watched meeting lasted about an hour and a half late Thursday afternoon China time, following a working lunch between Trump and Xi that started at least an hour later than originally planned. U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on November 19, 2026 in Shenzhen, China.Win Mcnamee | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesTrump told Xi and Putin they were "really making history" with the first-ever trilateral meeting between the three countries' leaders. He said it was an "honor" to be at the meeting with Putin and Xi, whom he congratulated on a "very successful APEC summit." The three were among the world leaders attending the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit."Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," Trump added. "We feel the opposite."Xi's 'correct' international diplomacy At the trilateral, Xi said that for large nations, having good interactions is not a choice but a necessity, according to a translation by state media.China's President Xi Jinping (C), U.S. President Donald Trump (R) and Russia's President Vladimir Putin (L) take part in a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong Province, on November 19, 2026. (Photo by Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)Mandel Ngan | Afp | Getty ImagesIn the report, Xi noted China's partnership with Russia, work towards constructive strategic stability in U.S. relations, and called on the three countries to respond to the world's challenges.Xi laid out four "correct" ways for large countries to interact: mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, and adherence to dialogue, according to state media.The Chinese president echoed Trump's comments on nuclear weapons, calling for such arms to be comprehensively prohibited and destroyed, adding that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.Putin said Russia, China and the U.S. can strengthen global stability if they cooperate constructively, calling for the three leaders to discuss energy security and global and regional issues — including the war in Ukraine.Beijing only confirmed the closely watched meeting on Monday. The three leaders had briefly gathered Wednesday evening as part of a welcome banquet for the APEC leaders more broadly.

schema.headline: Trump, Xi, Putin said they plan to boost oil production, revamp UN after trilateral talks

title: Jensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloons
description: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum at the Kennedy Center in Washington, Nov. 19, 2025.Stefani Reynolds | Bloomberg | Getty
body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum at the Kennedy Center in Washington, Nov. 19, 2025.Stefani Reynolds | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe still-unraveling scandal of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affairs and the tech giant's potential role in its advanced semiconductor chips ending up in China present a legal minefield for Huang and Nvidia.Federal and state prosecutors and Nvidia employees may target Huang and the company in court, where some shareholders have already taken action.That's on top of a rapidly growing pile of probes by Republicans who control Congress now and Democrats who will have majorities in both the House and Senate come January."It's not going to get any better for Jensen Huang; it's going to get far worse," said Salvatore Graziano, a New York securities litigation attorney at Bernstein, Litowitz, Berger & Grossmann. His firm is looking at shareholder lawsuit opportunities against Nvidia and Huang.[Huang] "faces the Department of Justice, the Securities and Exchange Commission and private litigation," Graziano said. "The criminal exposure is very serious. The SEC could bar him from being an officer. And the potential liability [from shareholder] lawsuits can be very large."Huang's and Nvidia's legal exposure stems from three issues that led up to his shock resignation Nov. 12.There's his alleged affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, who worked for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company under investigation for diverting advanced Nvidia semiconductor chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules. That, in turn, has raised questions about whether Huang and Nvidia were aware of any diversions.There are Huang's two other alleged affairs with Nvidia employees.And there is the sharp drop in the company's stock price in the wake of the scandal. Nvidia's share price has fallen 19% since Nov. 8, when Huang sent a company-wide apology acknowledging extramarital affairs.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia share priceHuang last week retained the law firm Paul, Weiss and its attorneys Melinda Haag and Walter Brown to represent him. Haag is a former U.S. attorney in San Francisco, and Brown is also a former federal prosecutor.Huang's spokesman at Trident, a crisis communications firm, declined to comment when asked if Haag and Brown are representing him in any potential criminal case and other questions about his legal exposure.Nvidia did not respond to a request for comment. Last week, Nvidia retained the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation into Huang allegedly being targeted by a spy, as U.S. intelligence reportedly has concluded.Read more CNBC news on NvidiaJensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloonsTrump bought Nvidia, Palantir, SpaceX amid federal contractsKress tells employees 'let's move forward' at first all-hands meeting since Huang exitPRO: Here's what every major Wall Street analyst is saying about Nvidia after its earnings reportKress tells Jim Cramer that 'customers continue to be with us'Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China access: SourcesThe civil liability Huang and Nvidia could face is underscored by a hearing Graziano, the securities attorney, attended Tuesday in U.S. District Court in San Francisco. A judge at the hearing approved a $175 million settlement from Seagate Technology Holdings to resolve a shareholder lawsuit alleging it concealed sales of hard-disk drives to Huawei in China in violation of export bans. The Seagate settlement came three years after the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security — which is investigating Megaspeed's business with Nvidia — imposed a $300 million penalty on Seagate for its sales to Huawei.Graziano said his law firm is "actively looking at securities law liability for Nvidia, Jensen Huang and other senior executives in the company given all the recent developments regarding their [potential] knowledge and facilitation of illegal chip sales to Chinese entities." One shareholder suit has been filedThere is already a pending class-action shareholder lawsuit in San Francisco federal court against Nvidia and Huang by the Rosen Law Firm, for allegedly misleading and false statements related to Megaspeed and Alice Huang. "Several hundreds of investors have contacted us and expressed an interest to join the case — investors of all walks of life, from mom and pops to investors with very large losses," Rosen attorney Phil Kim told CNBC in an email. Katie Sweeten, a former federal prosecutor in the DOJ's National Security Division, said the question of "who knew what and when, and what was [Huang's] role" is potentially the biggest risk for Nvidia and him."Now DOJ can leverage their criminal authorities," Sweeten, a partner at Scale LLP, told CNBC's Kelly Evans on "The Exchange.""They can bring grand jury subpoenas, search warrants for emails, bank accounts, personal devices, computers, things like that," Sweeten said.While it is "not illegal to, you know, sleep with a spy ... it is illegal to pass certain types of information to a counterintelligence officer," she said.Sweeten also pointed to potential export control violations, which "could be very serious."She noted the DOJ can indict a company as well as its officials if there is evidence of criminality. Export control violations carry a maximum possible criminal sentence of 20 years in prison and "really large fines," she said."You can't send the company to prison, but they can face fines, civil penalties, debarment — where you can't export items down the line," she said.One example of that came in July 2025, when the DOJ obtained a guilty plea and an agreement to pay more than $140 million from Cadence Design Systems for violating the Export Control Reform Act by unlawfully exporting semiconductor design tools to China's National University of Defense Technology, a school led by China's Central Military Commission.Congressional hearings present riskAnother potential legal risk for Huang comes from his planned appearances before Congress.Huang is scheduled to give a closed-door interview Dec. 1 to three House committees. Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., wants Huang's testimony before that panel to be public, and told CNBC Tuesday he hopes to have that happen "before Christmas."Sweeten said Huang "has to be very careful" about what he says there because of the risk of being criminally charged with lying to Congress, and of saying something "that absolutely can become part of a criminal or civil investigation.""I expect Huang to take the Fifth on most questions" from Congress, Jonathan Kanter, a former assistant attorney general in the DOJ's Antitrust Division, told CNBC, meaning Huang will likely use his constitutional right against giving testimony that could be used against him in a criminal case."With a Justice Department criminal investigation into Megaspeed already underway and more investigations possible, anything he tells Congress could be used against him," Kanter said. "His lawyers are likely to advise him against taking that risk."Ben Heineman Jr., a former senior vice president and general counsel of General Electric, and a senior fellow at Harvard University, told CNBC that Nvidia's board will be scrutinized over its actions before it pushed Huang to resign.Heineman cited the board's apparent lack of succession planning and what looks like weak oversight of Huang, including relating to personal conduct such as the two alleged affairs with Nvidia employees and with an executive of an Nvidia customer."When there is a sort of reasonable suspicion, they need to investigate it, and they don't appear to have done that," Heineman said.State attorneys general may circleNvidia and Huang could face investigation from state attorneys general, including in California, where the company is headquartered.On Tuesday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta told Bloomberg Television that the situation at Nvidia with Huang is "something that we're interested in." Bonta's office later told CNBC, "We are monitoring the situation."Huang's alleged affairs with Nvidia employees also open the possibility of workplace litigation.Ari Wilkenfeld, a Washington-area employment lawyer, said a consensual relationship between a chief executive and a subordinate "is not in and of itself illegal.""The liability never comes from the existence of the relationship alone. It comes from whether it was genuinely welcome, what job benefits flowed from it, and what it did to everyone else in the building," Wilkenfeld said. "California law recognizes that so-called sexual favoritism can create a hostile environment for an entire workforce."The affair is Huang's problem," Wilkenfeld said. "What, if anything, Nvidia did once it knew is the company's problem."

schema.headline: Jensen Huang's — and Nvidia's — legal exposure balloons

title: SoftBank plunges over 16% as AI sell-off hits Asian tech stocks following Anthropic debut
description: The SoftBank Group logo is displayed on a mobile phone with a stock graph in the background, in this photo illustration in Brussels, Belgium, on Augus
body: The SoftBank Group logo is displayed on a mobile phone with a stock graph in the background, in this photo illustration in Brussels, Belgium, on August 20, 2025. (Photo by Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto via Getty Images)Nurphoto | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesShares of Japan's SoftBank Group plunged 16.16% on Friday, leading a broader sell-off in Asian technology stocks following the highly anticipated market debut of artificial intelligence startup Anthropic.SoftBank is one of the biggest backers of OpenAI, Anthropic's rival, having invested a total of $64.6 billion in the ChatGPT maker.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconShares of SoftBank on 20 Nov. The sharp decline underscores growing investor concerns over SoftBank's aggressive bets on artificial intelligence, particularly its exposure to OpenAI, as markets question whether massive investments in AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns. SoftBank's heavy exposure to OpenAI has made its shares particularly sensitive to shifts in sentiment toward the AI sector. The stock lost 30% in October and is down 31% so far this month.If Friday's losses hold, it would be SoftBank's worst day in more than two years.Japanese semiconductor stocks also tumbled, with Tokyo Electron falling 7.19%, Lasertec declining 6.75% and Renesas Electronics dropping 6.71%. The sell-off extended to South Korea, where Nvidia suppliers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dropped 6% and 4.7%, respectively, pressuring the benchmark Kospi, which fell 4.6%. Elsewhere in the region, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, or TSMC, fell 4.76% in Taiwan. Chinese tech giant Tencent declined 1.89%, while memory chipmaker CXMT fell 4.35% to a fresh record low, while Baidu dropped 4.42%. AI chipmaker Enflame, dubbed as one of China's "four little dragons" fell 3.93%.The declines in Asia come after the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% overnight following Anthropic's highly anticipated Wall Street debut.

schema.headline: SoftBank plunges over 16% as AI sell-off hits Asian tech stocks following Anthropic debut

title: Palo Alto stock jumps on earnings beat and company's big bet on securing open-weight models
description: Palo Alto Networks shares rose 6% on Thursday as businesses boosted spending on cybersecurity products and investors cheered the company's acquisition
body: Palo Alto Networks shares rose 6% on Thursday as businesses boosted spending on cybersecurity products and investors cheered the company's acquisition of a startup that pushes it into securing open-weight artificial intelligence models.The company beat Wall Street's estimates for the fiscal first quarter. Revenue jumped 39% from a year ago and Palo Alto lifted its guidance for the year. Recent outages at Microsoft, banks and the Federal Aviation Administration have left businesses reeling. While U.S. officials haven't detected any malicious activity, the disruptions raise concerns over aging equipment and infrastructure. Many businesses are scrambling to patch vulnerabilities at a faster clip than ever before to keep pace with the growing risks of AI-powered cyberattacks. Those fears have led more businesses to consolidate platforms, which is fueling growth in areas like firewall and AI security, Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora told CNBC's "Mad Money" on Wednesday. "They're going to have to make sure they get the best players in the market to come support them because this is no longer child's play," Arora said. Read more CNBC tech newsFollow CNBC's live coverage of Anthropic's IPO and Nasdaq debutAnthropic IPO: AI lab considers increasing the offering as investor demand surges, sources sayWith Jensen Huang gone, Colette Kress shows Nvidia is still at the center of AIOne of AI’s most notorious ‘doomers’ stands to make billions in Anthropic’s IPOWidespread outages hit banks, air travel, the NSA and Apple, disrupting seemingly everythingAlongside earnings, Palo Alto announced a $4.5 billion deal to buy Applied Compute, a startup that helps train customized open-weight models. It's one of several recent deals in Arora's aggressive acquisition spree and marks a significant shift beyond cybersecurity. "Rather than being one player out of 10 in the industry serving compute, we want to be the one player with Palo Alto that delivers secure compute and security capability," Arora told CNBC. Palo Alto expects the deal to add more than $1 billion in annual recurring revenue to its next-generation security business by the 2029 fiscal year. Analysts at Bank of America touted the deal as a "bold move" to expand beyond securing AI into training open-weight models, allowing Palo Alto to lead the next phase of the AI revolution.This "appears consistent with PANW's 'long-game' - become indispensable beyond cyber into multidisciplinary IT domains across AI-value-chain," wrote analysts at Citigroup.WATCH: Palo Alto Networks shares surgewatch now

schema.headline: Palo Alto stock jumps on earnings beat and company's big bet on securing open-weight models
